info.bio: Este grupo se formó a principios de la decada de 1990 en la ciudad de San Diego, Estados Unidos. Enmarcados en la tendencia Grunge, fueron contemporáneos de Pearl Jam, Nirvana, Alice in chains, Soundgarden y Faith No More, entre otros. A pesar de sufrir notorias acusaciones de copiar el estilo de otros grupos (sobre todo a Pearl Jam), gracias a su single "Plush" Stone Temple Pilots sobrevive a las feroces críticas y escribe su particular página

scenes.desc: El grunge, revival del hard rock de los setenta y renacimiento musical de Seattle, fue uno de los grandes fenómenos de los noventa (casi solo en EE UU). Green River lo inauguran (Come On Down) y Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, Melvins y Mudhoney fijan sus cuatro puntos cardinales; Nirvana, con Nevermind, lo convierten en una tragaperras y en la banda sonora de la crisis nerviosa de una generación. Después, Alice In Chains (Dirt), Foo Fighters, Hammerbox, GodHeadSilo, Everclear, Stone Temple Pilots, Tool (el grupo más innovador de la segunda generación: Aenima, Lateralus), God Machine, Helmet, Quicksand, Urge Overkill, los Smashing Pumpkins (Siamese Dream, Mellon Collie), Scarce, Creed, Bush, Manic Street Preachers, Silverchair.

podcast.title: Formation (1986)
podcast.body: Stone Temple Pilots formed in San Diego in 1986, with founders Scott Weiland and bass player Robert DeLeo. Robert's brother Dean (guitar) and Eric Kretz (drums) joined later. "STP formed in San Diego in 1986. Wyland and bass player Robert DeLay are were the founders."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formation (1986)
podcast.body: Stone Temple Pilots was founded in San Diego in 1986 by Scott Weiland, who sang and wrote most of the lyrics, and bassist Robert DeLeo. "STP was formed in San Diego, fined by Wyland and bass player Robert Delio in 1986."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lollapalooza 1992 Second Stage Act
podcast.body: Stone Temple Pilots were among the bands featured on the second stage at selected dates during the 1992 Lollapalooza Festival, which boasted a critically acclaimed lineup. "You could have seen the stone type of pilots rage against the machine, Cypress Hill."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Heroin Addiction (1993)
podcast.body: Scott Weiland's heroin addiction began around 1993, with a story claiming Butthole Surfers' Gibby Haynes introduced him to it during a tour. This addiction created "all kinds of problems for the band." "The story is that during an STP tour with the Butthole surfers, the surfers Gibby Haynes showed Scott how it was done."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Scott Weiland's Drug Addiction (1993 Onwards)
podcast.body: Scott Weiland discovered heroin in 1993, allegedly introduced by Gibby Haynes of the Butthole Surfers during a tour. This marked the beginning of his cycle of substance abuse, leading to repeated stints in rehab and jail starting in 1995. "Then in 1993, Wyland discovered that he really liked heroin. The story is that during a tour with the Butthole Surfers, singer Gibby Haynes gave Scott a taste and then, you know, whether the story is true or not doesn't matter because Wyland did get into heroin."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Drug-Fueled Recording of Purple (1994)
podcast.body: The recording of the "Purple" album in Atlanta was notably swift, completed in just four weeks, largely because Scott Wyland's local dealer, a 25-year-old HIV-positive woman, supplied him with drugs that prevented him from becoming "dope sick," thus enabling continuous work. "Her stuff kept Scott from getting dope sick, which meant that the album was recorded rather quickly, four weeks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rehab and Jail Stints (1995-1998)
podcast.body: Throughout 1995, Scott Weiland was frequently in and out of rehab and jail. In 1998, he was arrested on a possession charge and sentenced to a year in jail. "During 1995 Wyland was in and out of rehab and in and out of jail. And then in 1998 he was nabbed on a possession charge and sentenced to a year in jail."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Weiland's Legal Issues (1995-2008)
podcast.body: Weiland's legal troubles began in 1995 with an arrest for attempting to buy crack. In 1998, he was jailed for a possession charge. In December 2007, he received another DUI charge, resulting in an 18-month alcohol rehab program, four years probation, and eight days in jail (of which he served about 10 hours). He attended rehab for three weeks in January 2008. "Starting in 1995, Wyland was in and out of rehab and in and out of jail, starting with a bust involving an attempt to buy some crack."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Fit and Ready to Rock" Reunion Press Conference (October 1, 1996)
podcast.body: At the same location where they announced Scott Wyland's departure, Stone Temple Pilots held a press conference on October 1, 1996, declaring that all members were "fit and ready to rock" after Wyland's drug treatment. Scott expressed the importance of his bandmates, stating, "It's an important thing to me to have these guys in my life. It's a relationship. It's not just about the band and business."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Isolation for Writing Tiny Music (1996)
podcast.body: For their third album, the band rented actor Jimmy Stewart's mansion in Santa Barbara, believing the isolation would benefit everyone, particularly Scott Wyland, in their writing process. Despite this, Wyland frequently traveled down the Pacific Coast Highway to Los Angeles to purchase cocaine and heroin. "He was thought that the isolation would do everyone, especially Scott, a lot of good."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Public Statement on Tour Cancellation (April 1996)
podcast.body: Stone Temple Pilots issued a public statement clarifying the cancellation of their tour dates, explicitly attributing it to Scott Wyland's "dependency on drugs" and his being "under a doctor's care in a medical facility." The statement emphasized that it was not due to typical reasons like exhaustion, dehydration, or a sore throat. "Our lead singer, Scott Wyland has become unable to rehearse or appear for these shows due to his dependency on drugs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Scott Wyland's Temporary Departure (1996)
podcast.body: Scott Wyland was effectively "out" of Stone Temple Pilots after the band suggested he pay millions in restitution for the canceled tour dates, a period that coincided with the end of his marriage to Janina. "And that was it for STP as Scott was concerned. He was out, especially after he was suggested that he pay some kind of restitution for the canceled dates out of his own pocket, which meant millions."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Six-Week Road Trip with Guardian (November 4 - December 14, 1996)
podcast.body: The band embarked on a six-week road trip beginning November 4 in Los Angeles, concluding in Cleveland on December 14. Scott Wyland was required to be accompanied by a guardian and adhere to a nightly curfew, with a decision made to avoid crossing international borders to minimize potential hassles with customs due to Wyland's history. "Wyland was to be accompanied by a guardian and was required to meet a nightly curfew."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Tour Cancellation Due to Scott Wyland's Addiction (1996-1997)
podcast.body: The band was forced to cancel a substantial portion of their tour supporting "Tiny Music" throughout late 1996 and into 1997 due to Scott Wyland's persistent drug issues and his inability to rehearse or perform. The band stated, "Our lead singer is a junkie with the message and we can't go on the road with him until he's well."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Breakup and Temporary Hiatus (1997)
podcast.body: Following the Toronto show in 1997, three-quarters of the band parted ways with Scott Weiland due to his ongoing personal struggles with drugs, legal issues, and domestic problems. This was acknowledged as a necessary break for everyone to sort things out creatively, musically, physically, mentally, and legally, though not necessarily permanent. "Following the show, three quarters of the band and Wyland parted ways."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Impact of Scott's Relapse on Album Charts (January 1997)
podcast.body: Scott Wyland's relapse and subsequent undetermined rehab stay came at a time when "Tiny Music" had significantly climbed the album charts, jumping 78 spots in a month due to the recent tour, causing frustration for the other band members. "Tiny music had jumped 78 spots on the album charts in a month because of the tour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Manager's Statement on Scott's Relapse (January 6, 1997)
podcast.body: On January 6, 1997, STP's manager Steve Stewart issued a statement confirming Scott Wyland was having problems again and was seeking care, but assured that he was safe, not arrested, and the band remained together. "Scott has made the band aware that he was having problems again and is taking care of himself at this point."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Tour Cancellations (January 1997)
podcast.body: Following a successful six-week tour, Stone Temple Pilots canceled a New Year's show in Anchorage, Alaska, without explanation, and two subsequent shows in Hawaii for the first week of January 1997, disappointing over 30,000 fans. "Then two more shows scheduled for the first week in January and Hawaii were also blown out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rumors of Disbandment (May 25, 1997)
podcast.body: After a show in Toronto on May 25, 1997, rumors began to circulate that Stone Temple Pilots were "finished for good." "After a show in Toronto on May 25th, 1997, the rumors were that the Stone Temple pilots were finished for good."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hiatus and Talk Show Project (1998)
podcast.body: In 1998, the band went on a hiatus aimed at helping Scott Weiland get clean. During this break, the other three members formed a new project called Talk Show with singer David Coutts, which ultimately "did not work out very well," leading to STP's reunion in its original form. "At that point, the other three quarters of STP formed a new project called Talk Show with the singer named David Coots, which did not work out very well and STP was tuned back together in its original form."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

podcast.title: Multiple DUIs and Bizarre Arrest (1998)
podcast.body: Scott Weiland had a history marked by numerous DUIs. In a particularly bizarre incident in 1998, he was arrested while attempting to purchase crack cocaine, at the time dressed as a pimp. "Scott Wyland, so many DUIs, and then there was the time in 1998 when he was arrested trying to buy a crack while dressed as a pimple."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Canceled Gigs Due to Probation Violation (June 1999)
podcast.body: A gig scheduled for June 11 in New York City was canceled after Impact House reported Scott Wyland's probation violation, leading to Judge Fiddler ordering him back to rehab. "A gig in New York City, Schedule for June 11th was canceled, and there was a matter of a show set for Las Vegas in August the 12th."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Las Vegas Show Before Incarceration (August 12, 1999)
podcast.body: The band performed an acclaimed show in Las Vegas on August 12, 1999, which became Scott Wyland's "last night of freedom" before he had to turn himself in for sentencing. The band described the experience as surreal, witnessing their friend taken away by a bailiff the next morning after a great performance. "We watched our friend be taken away by a 200 pound bailiff, man. It was the most surreal four days you'd ever want to experience."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lollapalooza Headliner Rumors (March 1999)
podcast.body: Following positive progress reports on Scott Wyland in March 1999, rumors suggested that Stone Temple Pilots would headline Lollapalooza if the festival were to be reactivated. "There were rumors that if Lola Paloza were to be reactivated, STP would be the headliners."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reunion and Renewed Chemistry (February 1999)
podcast.body: After their separate projects, the other three members realized the importance of their collective "chemistry" and Dean DeLeo called Scott Wyland, who, feeling "out of options," agreed to rejoin. They entered the studio in February 1999 with Brendan O'Brien to work on their fourth album, "Number 4." "One of them was chemistry. We looked at each other in a different way and thought, this is what we mean to each other."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Comeback Plans (March 2000)
podcast.body: By the end of March 2000, plans were being made for more showcase gigs, a tour, and even a pay-per-view event for the band, signaling a hopeful return to active touring and recording. "And by the end of the month, plans were in place for more showcase gigs, a tour, and even a pay-per-view event."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Promotional Acoustic Tour (Early 2000)
podcast.body: Following Scott Weiland's release from jail and rehab in January 2000, Stone Temple Pilots relaunched their "Number Four" album. For promotion, Scott Weiland and Dean DeLeo toured the US, performing acoustic versions of STP songs for radio stations and media outlets. "So for the relaunch, Scott and Dean Delayow went around the US playing acoustic versions of STP songs for radio stations and other media outlets."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: VH1 Special (March 8, 2000)
podcast.body: All four members of Stone Temple Pilots traveled to New York on March 8, 2000, to tape a special for the video channel VH1, marking a public appearance after Scott Wyland's recent release from jail and halfway house. "On March 8th, all four members of the band went to New York where they taped a special for VH1, the video channel."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Internal Tensions and Fights (2001)
podcast.body: During the 2001 tour, Scott Weiland's frequent unwellness led to increased tensions, arguments, and even physical fights among band members, culminating in a significant incident at the last show of the year in Texas on October 30th. "And because Scott seemed so unwell most of the time, tensions went up. There were fights."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lukewarm Album and Tour Reaction (2001)
podcast.body: The "Shangri-La Dee Da" album received a lukewarm reception from fans, and the accompanying tour was also not well-received. This likely contributed to intense backstage partying and heightened tensions within the band. "The overall reaction to the album was Luke Warm. The tour wasn't great either, which may have contributed to some extra hard backstage partying."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shangri-La Dee Da Single Dispute (2001)
podcast.body: The band and their record label disagreed on the first single for "Shangri-La Dee Da." The label insisted on the more commercial "Days of the Week," while the band preferred the rocker "Coma." The label ultimately prevailed. "The record company said, look, let's not push things. Let's just concentrate on making a solid single album, so you guys can get your career back on track."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Breakup (2002)
podcast.body: Following a fight between Scott Weiland and Dean DeLeo at the end of their 2002 tour, the band broke up. "Once he got out he rejoined STP but at the end of the 2002 tour Wyland got into a fight with Dean DeLay and that was it. The band broke up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hiatus/Breakup (End of 2002)
podcast.body: By the end of 2002, Stone Temple Pilots effectively ceased to exist, entering a hiatus that many perceived as a breakup due to ongoing internal issues and Scott Weiland's personal struggles. "Whatever word you want to use, the Stone Tip of Pond's effectively ceased to be as of the end of 2002."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Initial Breakup (2002)
podcast.body: Following more turbulent years, Stone Temple Pilots broke up in 2002. "There are more tumultuous years followed and then the band broke up in 2002."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

podcast.title: Initial Breakup (End of 2002 Tour)
podcast.body: The band broke up at the conclusion of their 2002 tour after Scott Weiland got into a fight with Dean DeLeo. "Then at the end of STP's 2002 tour, he got into a fight with Dean Delio. That was it. The band broke up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Initial Breakup (End of 2002 Tour)

podcast.title: Initial Breakup (End of 2002 Tour)

podcast.title: Assumed Demise (2003)
podcast.body: As of 2003, there was a widespread assumption that Stone Temple Pilots were "dead" and would no longer release new music, given the band's turbulent history and Scott Weiland's chronic problems. "As we moved into 2003, the assumption was that the Stone Temple Pond were dead and that we'd hear nothing more from them anymore."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Gradual Dissolution (September 1, 2003)
podcast.body: The band's initial breakup was gradual, without a formal announcement, as they "just quietly evaporated." "The best I can tell, STP was done by about September 1st 2003."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Scott Weiland's Issues and Alignment (2003+)
podcast.body: Scott Weiland had personal issues and aligned himself against the DeLeo brothers, contributing to the band's quiet demise. "Scott Wyand had his issues and he had lined himself against the Delayo brothers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Reunion and Dual Membership (2006)
podcast.body: Stone Temple Pilots reunited in 2006 after being offered a substantial sum of money. Scott Weiland attempted to divide his time between STP and Velvet Revolver, an arrangement noted as "probably not the best." "In 2006, STP was offered a whole bunch of money to reunite, which they did, with Wyland dividing his time between them and Velvet Revolver."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reunion for Financial Offer (2006)
podcast.body: Stone Temple Pilots reunited in 2006 after being offered "a big pile of money," with Scott Weiland intending to divide his time between STP, Velvet Revolver, and solo work. "But then in 2006 STP was offered a big pile of money to reunite, which they did."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mary Forsberg's Reunion Catalyst (2007)
podcast.body: Scott Weiland's estranged wife, Mary Forsberg, initiated a potential reunion by calling the DeLeo brothers to invite them to play a private party. "The story is that Mary Forsberg, who by the way is now Wyland's estranged wife, she called the Delayo brothers and she said, hey, you know, we're having this private party, you want to come over and play?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Promoter Offers for Reunion (2007)
podcast.body: Around the same time, promoters floated offers for the band to reform for a series of festivals, offering "decent coin," which led to the belief that a reunion was a "done deal" though nothing immediately materialized. "Around the same time some offers had been floated from promoters, offering decent coin if the band would reform for a series of some refesibles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Plan for New Album (Late 2008)
podcast.body: After successfully completing their 73-show reunion tour in 2008, Stone Temple Pilots agreed to try and make another album. "And when it was done, it was agreed that they should try to make another album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reconciliation and Reunion Tour (2008)
podcast.body: Following Scott Weiland's departure from Velvet Revolver, Mary Forsberg organized a party featuring the DeLeo brothers where a "big reconciliation" occurred, leading to Stone Temple Pilots' return. A promoter offered substantial money for a series of shows from June to December 2008, which the band successfully completed, performing 73 shows. "And suddenly, STP was back in business. A promoter offered some big dollars that the band could hold it together long enough to play a long series of shows from June to December 2008, and to everyone's surprise they did."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reformation Date (April 15, 2008)
podcast.body: After extensive investigation, this date is cited as the best estimate for when Stone Temple Pilots reformed. "Well, after all kinds of digging, the best date I can come up with is about April 15th, 2008."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Scott Weiland Arrived Separately at Edgefest (2008)
podcast.body: During the 2008 reunion tour, Scott Weiland often arrived at gigs, such as Edgefest in Toronto, separately from his bandmates. This was "standard operating procedure" at the time, employed to help maintain a fragile peace within the group. "Scott arrived separately from his other bandmates, standard operating procedure in those days to help keep the fragile peace."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Scott Weiland Quits Velvet Revolver (March 21, 2008)
podcast.body: Weiland surprised his Velvet Revolver bandmates by announcing mid-show that this would be his last tour with them, freeing him up for a potential STP reunion. "On March 21st, 2008, Wyland announced in the middle of a Velvet Revolver show that this would be his last tour with the band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Atlantic Records Suggests New Album (2009)
podcast.body: Following the success of the 2008-2009 reunion tour, Atlantic Records, Stone Temple Pilots' former label, suggested it was time for the band to record another album, nine years after "Shangri-La Dee Da," due to renewed momentum. "The 2008-2009 STP reunion tour went well enough for Atlantic STP's old record label to suggest that it was time for another album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chester Bennington Joins (2013)
podcast.body: In May 2013, after firing Scott Weiland, the band announced that Chester Bennington of Linkin Park would join as a full-time member. This arrangement lasted about 18 months, during which they toured extensively and released one 5-track EP. "In May of that year, they announced that Chester Bennington of Lincoln Park was the new guy and as a full-time member too."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

podcast.title: Chester Bennington Joins (2013)
podcast.body: In May 2013, Chester Bennington became a full-fledged member of Stone Temple Pilots, performing in Los Angeles. Dean DeLeo praised Chester's "one-of-a-kind voice," while Chester expressed his lifelong admiration for the band, noting their significant influence on him. Linkin Park's members were supportive of this venture. "But then in May 2013, the group took the stage in Los Angeles. In Outfront, not as a temporary lead singer or a guest, but as a full-fledged member of the band was Chester Bennington."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chester's Tenure & Departure (2013-2015)
podcast.body: Chester toured and recorded with Stone Temple Pilots for two and a half years before amicably departing in November 2015. He cited the inability to dedicate the necessary time to both STP and Linkin Park, alongside family needs, as the reason for his departure. He expressed a desire to focus solely on Linkin Park to give 100%. "So for the next two and a half years, Chester toured and recorded with Stone Tipple pilots."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Firing of Scott Weiland (February 27, 2013)
podcast.body: On February 27, 2013, Stone Temple Pilots officially terminated Scott Weiland, issuing a one-line statement. This decision came as the band believed Weiland had reverted to his old ways with drug abuse. This led to "back and forth lawsuits" before settling. "Even temple pilots have announced they have officially terminated Scott Wyland. In other words, they fired him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Scott Weiland Fired (2013)
podcast.body: After another reunion that lasted until 2013, Scott Weiland, still out of control due to his issues, was fired from Stone Temple Pilots on February 27, 2013. The band retained the rights to their name, intending to continue with a more reliable singer. "Wyland was still out of control. He was fired on February 27th of 2013."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

podcast.title: Scott Weiland's Departure (2013)
podcast.body: In February 2013, Scott Weiland was removed from the band due to excessive drug and alcohol use and ongoing drama, leading many to believe it would mark the end of Stone Temple Pilots. "In February of 2013, Scott Wyland was kicked out of the Stone Tipple pilots. Too many drugs, too much alcohol, too much drama."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Scott Weiland's Firing (2013)
podcast.body: On February 27, 2013, Stone Temple Pilots "officially terminated Scott Wyland" with a one-line statement, citing his continued drug issues and chronic lateness. Weiland responded by claiming he couldn't be fired as he was a founder of the group. "Stone Temple Pilots have announced that they have officially terminated Scott Wyland."

podcast.title: Scott Weiland's Official Termination (February 27, 2013)
podcast.body: On February 27, 2013, the band officially terminated Scott Weiland with a one-line statement, following persistent drug issues and his habitual lateness for engagements. Weiland countered by claiming they couldn't fire him from "his band," leading to legal involvement. "On February 27, 2013, he was sacked with this one-line statement. Stone Temple Pilots have announced that they have officially terminated Scott Wyland."

podcast.title: Chester Bennington Departs (2015)
podcast.body: Chester Bennington amicably left Stone Temple Pilots on November 9, 2015, to return to Linkin Park. The initial plan was for him to rejoin STP after completing Linkin Park's next project. "Chester left the group amicably on November 9th, 2015 to go back to Lincoln Park."

podcast.title: LA County Jail Detox Wing Experience
podcast.body: As Inmate 615-8735 in the detox wing of the LA County Jail, Scott Weiland was assigned a dormitory bunk and followed a strict daily regimen. xref.title: Death by Mixed Drug Toxicity (December 3, 2015)
xref.body: Scott Weiland died on December 3, 2015, at the age of 48, with the cause ruled an accident due to mixed drug toxicity (cocaine, ethanol/alcohol, and MDA). His death did not come as a surprise, given his long history of drug and alcohol offenses, rehab, and jail stints. He lived his life and career in "total chaos," constantly relapsing. After being kicked out of Stone Temple Pilots, he lost his support systems and suffered from manic episodes of paranoia and depression. In early 2015, rumors about his ill health were rampant. His managers reported seeing him use coke to drink more. He also faced personal issues, including his father and mother being diagnosed with cancer, and losing custody of his children to his second wife, Mary Forsberg. Financially "tapped out," touring was his only income. He was on six prescription drugs and had Hepatitis C, likely from heroin use. His death was similar to his brother's in 2007. "The result was mixed drug toxicity, cocaine, ethanol, which is alcohol, and the emphetamine MDA."

xref.title: Long History of Addiction (Pre-2015)

"He'd been in and out of rehab and in and out of jail on drug and alcohol offenses for years. He lived his life and conducted his career in total chaos."

xref.title: Final Texts and Plans (July 2017)
xref.body: In July 2017, while his wife Talinda and six children were on vacation in Arizona, Chester Bennington returned to Los Angeles on July 19, citing a television commercial shoot as the reason. Around the same time, he exchanged texts with Robert DeLeo of Stone Temple Pilots and Matt Sorum of Guns N' Roses, even floating the idea of performing with Sorum again in their band Kings of Chaos, with no alarm bells raised by anyone. "In July 2017, his wife, Talinda, and his family, he had six kids, went to Arizona on a vacation. But then on July 19th, he said he had to get back to LA."

xref.title: "My Second Album" Hidden Track
xref.body: Richard Peterson, a friend of the Stone Temple Pilots and an admirer of Johnny Mathis, performed a hidden track titled "My Second Album" on the band's "Purple Album". This comedic piece was intentionally included to poke fun at the common practice among bands of incorporating hidden tracks at the end of their CDs. "The performer is a guy named Richard Peterson, a friend of the band, and a big fan of Johnny Mathis, which explains why the song goes like this."

xref.title: Chronic Relapse and Post-STP Decline (Years Leading to Death)
xref.body: Scott Weiland had a long history of being in and out of rehab and jail for drug and alcohol offenses, characterized by a cycle of cleaning up and relapsing. After being kicked out of Stone Temple Pilots, his support systems dwindled, leading to increased manic episodes of paranoia and depression. In early 2015, despite his claims of 13 years of sobriety, solo performances suggested otherwise, and his managers reported seeing him use cocaine to enable more drinking. "He'd clean up, then relapse, over and over again. Now it was bad enough when he was with Stone Temple Pilots, but when they kicked him out, it looked like all his support systems were gone."

xref.title: Comparisons to Stone Temple Pilots
xref.body: Stone Temple Pilots were often criticized and categorized by critics as a "blatant Pearl Jam rip off," especially upon the release of their song "Plush." Scott Weiland, however, strongly disliked these comparisons, pointing out significant differences in fashion and stage presence, as he never wore flannel. "Others thought that STP was a metal band, especially after hearing songs like sex type thing."
